narrative:
The model predicted an 82.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors that strongly signaled a high risk of bar exam failure. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the most influential. Being in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3 grades pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. These two academic performance measures mattered more than anything else in your profile. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure.

Compared with students who were accepted, your first-year ranking (decile 1) was dramatically lower than their average of 6, your third-year ranking was well below their average of roughly 5.8, and your LSAT score of 21 sat far below the accepted students’ average of 37. These gaps in core academic indicators created a clear pattern the model interpreted as a strong likelihood of struggling on the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.9 (versus an accepted average of 3.23), family income, gender, race, and full-time status played much smaller roles and did not drive the rejection.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and retaking the LSAT to raise your score significantly. Consider targeted bar-prep resources or a post-baccalaureate program before reapplying. (248 words)
